Chemosh
kē'mosh
n. (the national god of Moab, called by Scripture the abomination of Moab; a high place was built for him by Solomon and defiled by Josiah)
From Hebrew Kemosh, of uncertain derivation, possibly connected with a root meaning to subdue. Moab is called “the people of Chemosh”, the nation being identified with the idol it served.

Biblical Definition

Chemosh is the god of Moab, and Scripture treats him with a mixture of contempt and deadly seriousness. Contempt, because he cannot save his own: “Woe to thee, Moab! thou art undone, O people of Chemosh: he hath given his sons that escaped, and his daughters, into captivity unto Sihon king of the Amorites” (Num 21:29). Seriousness, because his worship was the ruin of Israel's wisest king. “Then did Solomon build an high place for Chemosh, the abomination of Moab, in the hill that is before Jerusalem” (1Ki 11:7) — built by the man who had built the temple, on the hill facing it, for the wives who turned away his heart. The LORD named the offence when He tore the kingdom in two: “because that they have forsaken me, and have worshipped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, Chemosh the god of the Moabites, and Milcom the god of the children of Ammon” (1Ki 11:33). Three hundred years later Josiah went out and defiled those same high places, still standing on what Kings calls the mount of corruption (2Ki 23:13). Jephthah, negotiating with Ammon, speaks of Chemosh as the god the enemy believes gives him land (Jdg 11:24) — the diplomat's courtesy, not a concession; Jephthah's own confidence is in the LORD who is Judge.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Chemosh; in sacred history he is the national idol of the Moabites, called the abomination of Moab.

expand to see more

CHEMOSH, n. The chief idol of the Moabites, and reckoned also among the gods of Ammon.

Moab is called in the book of Numbers the people of Chemosh.

Solomon built an high place for Chemosh on the hill before Jerusalem, for his strange wives.

For this and the like idolatries the kingdom was rent from his son.

Josiah defiled the high places which Solomon had builded, on the mount of corruption.

Key Scripture

Num 21:29 — "Woe to thee, Moab! thou art undone, O people of Chemosh: he hath given his sons that escaped, and his daughters, into captivity unto Sihon king of the Amorites."

1Ki 11:7 — "Then did Solomon build an high place for Chemosh, the abomination of Moab, in the hill that is before Jerusalem, and for Molech, the abomination of the children of Ammon."

1Ki 11:33 — "Because that they have forsaken me, and have worshipped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, Chemosh the god of the Moabites, and Milcom the god of the children of Ammon, and have not walked in my ways, to do that which is right in mine eyes, and to keep my statutes and my judgments, as did David his father."

Jdg 11:24 — "Wilt not thou possess that which Chemosh thy god giveth thee to possess? So whomsoever the LORD our God shall drive out from before us, them will we possess."

Modern Corruption

Israel's religion is described as one national cult among several — the LORD for Israel, Chemosh for Moab — when the Old Testament's whole claim is that the idols are nothing and the LORD alone is God.

expand to see more

A standard academic reading treats early Israel as henotheistic: each nation had its god, Chemosh belonged to Moab as the LORD belonged to Israel, and strict monotheism developed later. Jephthah's sentence about “Chemosh thy god” is the usual proof-text. It will not carry the weight. Jephthah is arguing with a pagan king in the king's own terms, as Paul quoted the Athenian poets without endorsing them, and he closes by appealing to “the LORD the Judge” over both nations. The Pentateuch itself, long before, is explicit: “the LORD he is God in heaven above, and upon the earth beneath: there is none else” (Deu 4:39). The idols are not rival deities; they are, as the psalmist says, the work of men's hands, and behind them, as Paul says, are devils and not God (1Co 10:20).

The second corruption is a failure to feel the horror of Solomon's high place. The wisest man who ever lived, who had seen the glory fill the house he built, put a shrine to the abomination of Moab on the facing hill because his wives wanted it. Kings does not say he stopped believing; it says “his wives turned away his heart” (1Ki 11:3). Syncretism rarely announces itself as apostasy. It arrives as accommodation, as peace in the household, as tolerance for what someone loved brought with them — and three centuries later a reforming king is still tearing out what one man permitted. “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1Jn 5:21) is the last sentence of John's epistle, written to Christians, not Moabites.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Kemosh (H3645), Chemosh; shiqquts (H8251), abomination, detestable thing; bamah (H1116), high place; 'elil (H457), idol, thing of nought; tame' (H2930), to defile.

expand to see more

Hebrew Kemosh (H3645) — Chemosh; the national idol of Moab.

Hebrew shiqquts (H8251) — detestable thing, abomination; Kings' standing word for him.

Hebrew bamah (H1116) — high place; what Solomon built and Josiah defiled.

Hebrew 'elil (H457) — idol, a thing of nought; the prophets' estimate of such gods.

Hebrew tame' (H2930) — to make unclean, defile; Josiah's treatment of the shrines.

Usage

"“O people of Chemosh” — a nation named after the idol that could not save it."

"“An high place for Chemosh… in the hill that is before Jerusalem” — facing the temple he built."

"“The abomination of Moab” — Scripture's settled name for him."
